```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`misskappa` estimates weighted agreement coefficients (Conger, Fleiss,
Brennan–Prediger) and coefficient alpha when some ratings are **missing**, and
attaches an asymptotic covariance matrix to every estimate so you get standard
errors, confidence intervals, and equality tests for free. Each estimator is
chosen with a single `estimator=` argument. You never have to remember a
combination of `method` and `type` flags.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(misskappa)
```

## A first agreement coefficient

`dat.gwet2014` is a small categorical rating matrix (20 subjects, five
raters, four categories) with some ratings missing (`NA`). The
inverse-probability-weighted (IPW) estimator is consistent under
missing-completely-at-random missingness:

```{r}
fit <- kappa(dat.gwet2014, estimator = "ipw", weight = "linear")
fit
```

The print method shows each coefficient with its standard error and a 95%
confidence interval. The object carries everything you need:

```{r}
coef(fit)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
```

### Confidence intervals

`confint()` gives natural-scale Wald intervals, or a variance-stabilizing
Fisher *z* interval that always stays inside `(-1, 1)`, useful when a
coefficient is close to the boundary:

```{r}
confint(fit)
confint(fit, transform = "fisher")
```

## Choosing an estimator

The right `estimator=` depends on the data and the missingness assumption:

| Input | `estimator` | Assumption |
|---|---|---|
| Categorical ratings | `"ipw"` | MCAR, rater-varying observation rates |
| Categorical ratings | `"cat_fiml"` | Ignorable (MCAR or MAR), saturated multinomial |
| Scored ratings (quadratic) | `"pairwise"` | MCAR, distribution-free, saturated covariance |
| Scored ratings (quadratic) | `"pairwise_cs"` | MCAR, distribution-free, compound-symmetry covariance |
| Scored ratings (quadratic) | `"nt_fiml"` | Ignorable, normal-theory, saturated covariance |
| Scored ratings (quadratic) | `"nt_fiml_cs"` | Ignorable, normal-theory, compound-symmetry covariance |

The scored estimators treat the categories as numbers and use the quadratic
loss. Pass the scores directly, or integer codes together with `values`.

The two normal-theory FIMLs differ only in the within-subject covariance they
fit. `"nt_fiml"` is *saturated* (an unrestricted covariance) and `"nt_fiml_cs"`
is *compound symmetry* `Sigma = psi J + e I`, the fixed-rater variance-component
model. Compound symmetry needs only a connected rater co-observation graph (not
every pair jointly observed) and is consistent and slightly more efficient when
that structure holds. It is also best-calibrated under MCAR even when the
covariance is misspecified. Prefer the saturated `"nt_fiml"` when the
missingness may be MAR and the covariance could depart from compound symmetry
(for example, rater subgroups with systematically different bias), where the
structured model can become inconsistent but the saturated one stays robust.
`"pairwise_cs"` is the distribution-free MCAR moment companion to `"nt_fiml_cs"`:
same compound-symmetry structure, no normality assumption. Because the
compound-symmetry estimators need only a *connected* co-observation graph, they
recover the coefficient on planned-incomplete designs where the saturated
estimators are not even identified. See `vignette("missingness-estimators")`.

```{r}
kappa(dat.zapf2016, estimator = "pairwise")
```

## Counts-format data

When raters are interchangeable and you only have per-subject category counts,
use `kappa_counts()`. `dat.fleiss1971` is the classic psychiatric-diagnosis
table (30 subjects, six raters, five categories):

```{r}
kappa_counts(dat.fleiss1971, estimator = "fleiss_cuzick")
```

## Coefficient alpha

`alpha()` estimates Cronbach's coefficient alpha for a subjects-by-items score
battery, again with missing entries allowed. `psych::bfi` is a 25-item Big Five
questionnaire answered by 2800 people, many of whom skipped at least one item.
Treating the five-item Neuroticism scale as the battery, the normal-theory FIML
estimator handles the missing responses under ignorable missingness:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("psych", quietly = TRUE)
data(bfi, package = "psych")
neuroticism <- bfi[, paste0("N", 1:5)]
sum(!complete.cases(neuroticism))      # respondents missing at least one item
alpha(neuroticism, estimator = "nt_fiml")
```

## Beyond pairwise: g-wise and vector-valued agreement

The same `kappa()` reaches two generalizations. Set `g > 2` for *g-wise*
agreement, where the disagreement kernel compares `g` raters at once (`g = 2` is
ordinary pairwise kappa):

```{r}
kappa(dat.gwet2014, estimator = "ipw", weight = "nominal", g = 3)
```

And when each rating is a *vector*, pass a subjects-by-raters-by-features array.
`dat.vanbelle2019` holds 28 observers classifying crackles at six chest sites
for 20 patients. A component loss (`weight`) measures vector disagreement:

```{r}
kappa(dat.vanbelle2019[, 1:4, ], estimator = "pairwise")
```

The [g-wise agreement](articles/gwise-agreement.html) article develops the
multirater kernels in full. Vector-valued agreement is in preparation: the
missing-data estimators are the same standard pairwise/IPW machinery used
elsewhere in the package, while the new work is the component-separable vector
loss family and full-matrix feature coupling. See the
[vector-valued agreement](articles/vector-valued-agreement.html) article.

## Testing whether coefficients are equal

A common question is whether a coefficient is the *same* across two groups, two
estimators, two timepoints, or several rater pairs. `kappa_test()` and
`alpha_test()` answer it and return a standard `htest`. Use `paired = TRUE`
(the default) when the fits share the same subjects (the dependence is taken
from the per-subject influence functions) and `paired = FALSE` for
independent samples.

```{r}
kappa_test(AB = kappa(dat.zapf2016[, 1:2], estimator = "pairwise"),
           CD = kappa(dat.zapf2016[, 3:4], estimator = "pairwise"),
           coef = "Conger")
```

See the [equality tests](articles/equality-tests.html) article for the
one-sample, independent, paired, and *G*-way homogeneity cases worked out on
real data, and the [mathematical guides](articles/index.html) for the
loss-matrix formulation and the missing-data estimators.
